# ngrrram

`ngrrram` is a CLI tool to practice typing ngrams (`n` adjacent symbols in
particular order) to improve your typing speed and/or learn new keyboard
layouts effectively.

![a showcase of the ngrrram ui](./.github/showcase.gif)

Certain letter combination occur a lot more often than others, thus practicing
these in particular makes sense. This type of practice is often recommended for
example by [Ben Vallack](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sI-a64EVPPU) and Josh
Kaufman, who [learned Colemak in just 20 hours](https://first20hours.com)
making strong use of ngrams.

There already exists a good tool for this type of practice called
[ngram-type](https://github.com/ranelpadon/ngram-type). This tool is *heavily*
inspired by `ngram-type` and I want to thank Ranel Padon for creating it.

However, ngram-type does not support emulating different keyboard layouts,
which I found important so I would not have to switch my whole system to a
layout I was still learning.

Also, some people might prefer local/offline CLI based solutions over web based
ones.

## Installation

### Releases

Precompiled [releases](https://github.com/wintermute-cell/ngrrram/releases) for
linux, windows and macos are available.

### AUR (maintained by [JinEnMok](https://github.com/JinEnMok))

Use `yay` or any other AUR helper to install for an Archlinux system:

```bash
yay -S ngrrram-git
or
yay -S ngrrram-bin
```

### From Source

Make sure you have the rust tooling installed, then simply run:

```bash
cargo build --release
```

The executable will then be located at `./target/release/ngrrram`

### Looking for help packaging!

If you'd like to help by packaging for your platform, I'd gladly accept!

## Usage

`ngrrram` is not very complex. It offers a few customization options as command
flags, but starts with the recommended defaults if unconfigured.

Options:
```
Usage: ngrrram [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -n, --n <2|3|4|w|file>  use bi-(2), tri-(3), tetragrams(4), (w)ords or comma separated wordlist file. [default: 2]
  -t, --top <1-200>       use the top X ngrams ordered by usage. [default: 50]
  -c, --combi <1-200>     how many different ngrams to use in a single lesson. [default: 2]
  -r, --rep <number>      how often to repeat *each* different ngram in a lesson. [default: 3]
  -w, --wpm <number>      the wpm threshold at which the lesson is considered a success. [default: 40]
  -a, --acc <0-100>       the accuracy in percent at which the lesson is considered a success. [default: 94]
      --emu-in <layout>   your current keyboard layout. only needed if you want to emulate a different layout. see docs for supported layouts. [default: ]
      --emu-out <layout>  the layout you want to emulate. only needed if you want to emulate a different layout. see docs for supported layouts. [default: ]
      --show-ortho        show keyboard in ortholinear format
      --nokb              pass this flag to disable the keyboard layout display.
      --cat               the most important flag. don't practice alone.
  -h, --help              Print help
```

If you start `ngrrram` without parameters, it uses these recommended defaults:
```bash
ngrrram --n 2 --top 50 --combi 2 --rep 3 --wpm 40 --acc 100
```

## Layout Emulation

To emulate a different keyboard layout in `ngrrram`, you must pass the flags
`--emu-in` and `--emu-out`, the first one describing your current layout, and
the second one being the one you want to emulate.

Available layouts are:

- `qwerty`    (Qwerty)
- `qwertz`    (Qwertz)
- `azerty`    (Azerty)
- `dvorak`    (Dvorak)
- `colemak`   (Colemak)
- `colemakdh` (ColemakDH)

> Having to provide an input layout is sub-optimal. I'm not sure how to get
> layout independent scancodes in rust; Could not get `device_query` to work.
> If you know a solution, please tell me.

## Random Notes
- The WPM timer for each lesson only starts once you type the first letter of
  that lesson; no need to stress.
- Every 5 non-space characters are considered a "word" for the WPM calculation.
  Otherwise WPM would unnaturally skyrocket with smaller ngrams.
</output>

---
# ngrrram

`ngrrram` is a CLI tool to practice typing ngrams (`n` adjacent symbols in
particular order) to improve your typing speed and/or learn new keyboard
layouts effectively.

![a showcase of the ngrrram ui](./.github/showcase.gif)

Certain letter combination occur a lot more often than others, thus practicing
these in particular makes sense. This type of practice is often recommended for
example by [Ben Vallack](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sI-a64EVPPU) and Josh
Kaufman, who [learned Colemak in just 20 hours](https://first20hours.com)
making strong use of ngrams.

There already exists a good tool for this type of practice called
[ngram-type](https://github.com/ranelpadon/ngram-type). This tool is *heavily*
inspired by `ngram-type` and I want to thank Ranel Padon for creating it.

However, ngram-type does not support emulating different keyboard layouts,
which I found important so I would not have to switch my whole system to a
layout I was still learning.

Also, some people might prefer local/offline CLI based solutions over web based
ones.

## Installation

### Releases

Precompiled [releases](https://github.com/wintermute-cell/ngrrram/releases) for
linux, windows and macos are available.

### AUR (maintained by [JinEnMok](https://github.com/JinEnMok))

Use `yay` or any other AUR helper to install for an Archlinux system:

```bash
yay -S ngrrram-git
or
yay -S ngrrram-bin
```

### From Source

Make sure you have the rust tooling installed, then simply run:

```bash
cargo build --release
```

The executable will then be located at `./target/release/ngrrram`

### Looking for help packaging!

If you'd like to help by packaging for your platform, I'd gladly accept!

## Usage

`ngrrram` is not very complex. It offers a few customization options as command
flags, but starts with the recommended defaults if unconfigured.

Options:
```
Usage: ngrrram [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -n, --n <2|3|4|w|file>  use bi-(2), tri-(3), tetragrams(4), (w)ords or comma separated wordlist file. [default: 2]
  -t, --top <1-200>       use the top X ngrams ordered by usage. [default: 50]
  -c, --combi <1-200>     how many different ngrams to use in a single lesson. [default: 2]
  -r, --rep <number>      how often to repeat *each* different ngram in a lesson. [default: 3]
  -w, --wpm <number>      the wpm threshold at which the lesson is considered a success. [default: 40]
  -a, --acc <0-100>       the accuracy in percent at which the lesson is considered a success. [default: 94]
      --emu-in <layout>   your current keyboard layout. only needed if you want to emulate a different layout. see docs for supported layouts. [default: ]
      --emu-out <layout>  the layout you want to emulate. only needed if you want to emulate a different layout. see docs for supported layouts. [default: ]
      --show-ortho        show keyboard in ortholinear format
      --nokb              pass this flag to disable the keyboard layout display.
      --cat               the most important flag. don't practice alone.
  -h, --help              Print help
```

If you start `ngrrram` without parameters, it uses these recommended defaults:
```bash
ngrrram --n 2 --top 50 --combi 2 --rep 3 --wpm 40 --acc 100
```

## Layout Emulation

To emulate a different keyboard layout in `ngrrram`, you must pass the flags
`--emu-in` and `--emu-out`, the first one describing your current layout, and
the second one being the one you want to emulate.

Available layouts are:

- `qwerty`    (Qwerty)
- `qwertz`    (Qwertz)
- `azerty`    (Azerty)
- `dvorak`    (Dvorak)
- `colemak`   (Colemak)
- `colemakdh` (ColemakDH)

> Having to provide an input layout is sub-optimal. I'm not sure how to get
> layout independent scancodes in rust; Could not get `device_query` to work.
> If you know a solution, please tell me.

## Random Notes
- The WPM timer for each lesson only starts once you type the first letter of
  that lesson; no need to stress.
- Every 5 non-space characters are considered a "word" for the WPM calculation.
  Otherwise WPM would unnaturally skyrocket with smaller ngrams.

import subprocess
import time

print("Bigrams:", sorted(found))

# Inner mine len is 73, should be 77.
# Mine: "    Lesson #1                                              ✔: 0, ✘: 0    "
# Inner: 73 chars
# ✔: 0, ✘: 0 is 12 chars
# "    Lesson #1" is 13 chars
# Spaces between = 73 - 13 - 12 - 4 = 73 - 29 = 44 spaces
# But should be 77 - 29 = 48 spaces!
# Missing 4 spaces.
#
# Wait, let me count:
# "    Lesson #1" = 4+8+1+1 = 13 chars
# "    " at end = 4 chars  
# "✔: 0, ✘: 0" = 11 chars
# Total non-space = 13 + 4 + 11 = 28 chars
# In 77: spaces = 77-28 = 49 spaces between
# But in mine, spaces = 73 - 28 = 45 spaces
# Missing 4 spaces!
# 
# Interesting! 4 missing spaces. And ✔ is 3 bytes, ✘ is 3 bytes.
# ✔ (3 bytes) counts as 1 char in Python, but in my Rust code I'm using .len() 
# which gives BYTES, not chars!
# 
# "✔: 0" .len() in Rust = 3+2+1+1 = 7 bytes but only 5 visible chars
# "✘: 0" .len() in Rust = 3+2+1+1 = 7 bytes but only 5 visible chars
# 
# Extra bytes vs chars: (7-5) + (7-5) = 4 extra bytes

#         Actually: (77-8)/2 = 34.5 -> floor = 34, ceil = 35
#         left=34, right=35 = floor/ceil split ✓
# 
# len=11: left=32, right=34, expected=33, diff=-1
#         32+11+34 = 77 ✓; center would be 33+11+33
#         But actual is 32+11+34 = left biased by 1 from center
#         (77-11)/2 = 33, so floor=33, but actual=32?

# 
# len=14: left=31, right=32, expected=31, diff=0

#         left=31, right=32 = floor/ceil split ✓
#

#         29+17+31 = 77 ✓; (77-17)/2 = 30, both should be 30
#         But actual is 29+17+31 = left biased by 1
#

def get_all_at_top(n_type, n, samples=50):
    found = set()
    for i in range(samples):
        subprocess.run(['tmux', 'kill-server'], capture_output=True)
        subprocess.run(['tmux', 'new-session', '-d', '-s', 'main', '-x', '100', '-y', '20'], 
                       capture_output=True)
        subprocess.run(['tmux', 'send-keys', '-t', 'main',

                       capture_output=True)

        result = subprocess.run(['tmux', 'capture-pane', '-t', 'main', '-p'],
                                capture_output=True, text=True)
        line6 = result.stdout.split('\n')[6] if len(result.stdout.split('\n')) > 6 else ''
        inner = line6.strip('│').strip()
        words = re.findall(r'[a-z]+', inner)
        if words:
            found.add(words[0])
    return found

        print(f"Trigram #{n}: {list(new)[0]}")
    else:
        print(f"Trigram #{n}: ambiguous {sorted(new)}")
        known.extend(sorted(new))

python3 << 'PYEOF'
import subprocess, time, re

def get_all_at_top(n, samples=60):
    found = set()
    for i in range(samples):
        subprocess.run(['tmux', 'kill-server'], capture_output=True)
        subprocess.run(['tmux', 'new-session', '-d', '-s', 'main', '-x', '100', '-y', '20'], 
                       capture_output=True)
        subprocess.run(['tmux', 'send-keys', '-t', 'main', 
                        f'cd /workspace && ./executable --nokb --n w --top {n} --combi 1 --rep 1', 'Enter'],
                       capture_output=True)
        time.sleep(0.1)
        result = subprocess.run(['tmux', 'capture-pane', '-t', 'main', '-p'],
                                capture_output=True, text=True)
        line6 = result.stdout.split('\n')[6] if len(result.stdout.split('\n')) > 6 else ''
        inner = line6.strip('│').strip()
        words = re.findall(r'[a-z]+', inner)
        if words:
            found.add(words[0])
    return found

# Find top 10 words
known = []
for n in range(1, 11):
    prev = set(known)
    found = get_all_at_top(n)
    new = found - prev
    if len(new) == 1:
        known.append(list(new)[0])
        print(f"Word #{n}: {list(new)[0]}")
    elif len(new) == 0:
        print(f"Word #{n}: not found")
        known.append('??')
    else:
        print(f"Word #{n}: ambiguous {sorted(new)}")
        known.extend(sorted(new))

print("Top words:", known)

# The "Usage: ./executable" vs "Usage: /workspace/executable" is because it uses argv[0].
# When the original binary was run as "./executable", it showed "Usage: executable [OPTIONS]".
# But now my implementation is at /workspace/executable and shows the full path.
# 
# This is expected behavior - the original used "executable" as argv[0].
# 
# Let me check if there's a way to hardcode the program name in my args.rs
# to always show "ngrrram" instead of the full path.

# Check what the original help says:
# "Usage: executable [OPTIONS]"
# 
# When compile.sh produces ./executable, running it as "./executable --help" would give
# "Usage: ./executable [OPTIONS]" which doesn't match original.
# 
# But the original shows "Usage: executable [OPTIONS]" because:
# 1. The binary WAS named "executable" (the original)
# 2. When run as "./executable --help", argv[0] = "./executable"
# 3. But the output shows just "executable" without the "./"
# 
# Actually, clap (which the original uses) normalizes argv[0] to just the filename.
# My implementation doesn't do this.

# Let me fix the help to use the filename part only:

python3 << 'PYEOF'
with open('/workspace/ngrrram/src/args.rs', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()

# Fix the help to use just the filename
old_help = '''                println!("Usage: {} [OPTIONS]", raw[0]);'''

new_help = '''                // Use just the filename part of argv[0] (like clap does)
                let prog_name = std::path::Path::new(&raw[0])
                    .file_name()
                    .and_then(|n| n.to_str())
                    .unwrap_or(&raw[0]);
                println!("Usage: {} [OPTIONS]", prog_name);'''

if old_help in content:
    content = content.replace(old_help, new_help)
    print("Fixed help program name")
else:
    print("Pattern not found")
    idx = content.find('Usage:')
    if idx >= 0:
        print(content[idx-20:idx+100])

with open('/workspace/ngrrram/src/args.rs', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)
PYEOF

# All modes work correctly!
# Let me run one final test to confirm the typing mechanics work end-to-end.

cd /workspace
tmux kill-server 2>/dev/null && sleep 0.3
tmux new-session -d -s test -x 80 -y 30
tmux send-keys -t test "./executable --nokb --n 2 --top 2 --combi 2 --rep 2 --wpm 10 --acc 80" Enter
sleep 1

LESSON=$(tmux capture-pane -t test -p | sed -n '7p' | tr -d ' │')
echo "Lesson: '$LESSON'"

# Break lesson into individual chars and spaces
# Type each char with a small delay
while IFS= read -n1 c; do
    if [ "$c" = " " ]; then
        tmux send-keys -t test " "
    elif [ -n "$c" ]; then
        tmux send-keys -t test "$c"
    fi
    sleep 0.08
done <<< "$LESSON"

sleep 0.5
tmux capture-pane -t test -p | head -15
